title: Seismology: Earthquake frequency

In a previous LiLyPad, you sketched a workflow to identify where earthquakes occur most frequently within a region.
Here, we use an earthquake catalog to investigate that question. The catalog is considered complete for earthquakes of magnitude 2.0 or greater between 2015 and 2024. We will select events that meet these criteria, count earthquakes within 10 × 10 km grid cells, and map their distribution.
As you work through the notebook, consider how the narrative, code, and results correspond to the data, analysis steps, and parameters in your sketch.

<b>Note:</b> Catalog completeness describes how reliably earthquakes are recorded. For this exercise, we assume that all earthquakes of magnitude 2.0 or greater within the study region were recorded during 2015–2024. Smaller earthquakes may be missing, so including them could make comparisons between locations misleading.

title: Seismology: Earthquake frequency
text:
Analysis
To compare earthquake counts across the region, we will divide it into 10 × 10 km grid cells. Our coordinates are currently in degrees of latitude and longitude, so we first express each earthquake’s location as a distance east and north of a reference point at 35°N, 120°W.
The resulting table retains the earthquake information and adds two columns: east_km and north_km.

<b>Note:</b> For this synthetic example, we use an approximate conversion from degrees to kilometers, accounting for longitude spacing at the reference latitude. Our grid cells are therefore approximately 10 × 10 km. For a real regional study, we would use a suitable projected coordinate system and document that choice.


LAT0 = 35.0
LON0 = -120.0
KM_PER_DEGREE = 111.195

spatial = selected.copy()

spatial["east_km"] = (
    (spatial["longitude"] - LON0)
    * KM_PER_DEGREE
    * np.cos(np.deg2rad(LAT0))
)

spatial["north_km"] = (
    (spatial["latitude"] - LAT0)
    * KM_PER_DEGREE
)

display(
    spatial[["event_id", "latitude", "longitude", "east_km", "north_km"]].head()
)

We divide our study region into cells approximately 10 km wide in both directions. The grid extends from 0 to 60 km east and north of our reference point, forming 36 cells.
We then count the earthquakes within each cell over the full 2015–2024 period. The result is a two-dimensional array, counts, containing one earthquake count per cell, including zeros where no events were recorded.

<b>Note:</b> Cell size, grid origin, and spatial extent are all choices that should be documented. Changing the boundaries can change which earthquakes are grouped together. Events on a boundary are assigned to the cell beginning at that boundary, except along the outermost edge, which is included in the final cell.


CELL_KM = 10
EXTENT_KM = 60

x_edges = np.arange(0, EXTENT_KM + CELL_KM, CELL_KM)
y_edges = np.arange(0, EXTENT_KM + CELL_KM, CELL_KM)

# Check that all selected earthquakes fall within our study region.
assert spatial["east_km"].between(0, EXTENT_KM).all()
assert spatial["north_km"].between(0, EXTENT_KM).all()

counts, x_edges, y_edges = np.histogram2d(
    spatial["east_km"],
    spatial["north_km"],
    bins=[x_edges, y_edges]
)

counts = counts.astype(int)

# Each earthquake should be counted exactly once.
assert counts.sum() == len(spatial)

print(f"Grid: {counts.shape[0]} × {counts.shape[1]} cells")
print(f"Total earthquakes counted: {counts.sum()}")
print(f"Highest count in a single cell: {counts.max()}")

Visualization
Let’s map the number of earthquakes recorded in each grid cell. The color shows the total count during 2015–2024, with brighter colors indicating more events. The axes show distances east and north of our reference point.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))

image = ax.pcolormesh(
    x_edges,
    y_edges,
    counts.T,
    cmap="viridis",
    shading="flat"
)

fig.colorbar(
    image,
    ax=ax,
    label="Earthquakes per cell (2015–2024)"
)

ax.set(
    xlabel="East of reference point (km)",
    ylabel="North of reference point (km)",
    title="Synthetic earthquake counts",
    aspect="equal"
)

fig.tight_layout()








The highest-count cells identify where earthquakes occurred most frequently in this synthetic catalog during our study period. This pattern depends on our magnitude threshold, time interval, and grid boundaries.
The map shows earthquake counts, not earthquake hazard. It does not account for differences in earthquake magnitude above our threshold or estimate the likelihood of future damaging events.

Our second step is to average measurements collected at the same station on the same date. Because the original team averaged these measurements before applying quality control (QC), we assign a QC flag of 1 to the average only if every measurement contributing to it has a QC flag of 1.

Now that you have a sense of what a scientific workflow is, let’s think about how workflows are different than software, even though both of them are often referred to as “code”. In short, Software is a tool. A workflow is the process in which tools are used.
Software performs particular tasks, such as reading data, calculating statistics, or creating a figure. A workflow connects data, actions, decisions, parameters, and outputs into a sequence that answers a scientific question. A workflow may use several software tools—and may also include manual steps that happen outside software.
A script or notebook can implement part (along with manual steps) or all of a workflow, but software and workflows are not interchangeable. Sharing the software does not necessarily reveal which data were used, what decisions were made, which parameters were selected, or what happened outside the software.

section: Git and GitHub are not the same thing
text:
Git and GitHub are not the same thing
Although their names are similar, Git and GitHub play different roles.
Git is a version-control system. It records changes to files over time, allowing you to examine the history of a project or return to an earlier version. Git can work locally on your computer without an internet connection.
GitHub is an online platform that hosts Git repositories. It also provides tools for sharing projects, discussing work, reviewing proposed changes, and organizing tasks.
A Git repository can exist without GitHub, and GitHub is not the only service that can host Git repositories.

title: Start a Research Repository
Release and Cite your Work
text:
You’ve created a research repository, tracked changes, collaborated through pull requests, and used Issues to organize your work. But how do you share a version of your research that someone else can reliably find, reuse, and cite?
A GitHub repository is a living project: files change, analyses evolve, and new features or corrections are added. A release identifies a particular version of that work, making it easier for others to understand exactly what was available at a given point in time.
In this Deep End Pad, you’ll prepare your repository for its first release. You’ll consider reuse permissions, create citation information, choose a version number, write release notes, and explore how GitHub releases can be preserved in a research archive such as Zenodo.
You’ll also discover why a GitHub release, an archived version with a DOI, a published dataset, and a research paper are not interchangeable—even when they are all part of the same research project.
The goal isn’t simply to make files available. It’s to help other researchers understand what you’ve shared, what they can do with it, and how to give your work appropriate credit.


By the end of this Pad, you will be able to:

Evaluate release readiness: Check whether your repository is sufficiently documented and identify scientific, technical, or permission-related issues that need attention.
Understand licensing: Recognize why a public repository isn’t automatically available for reuse and identify licensing questions for code, data, and documentation.
Create citation metadata: Add a CITATION.cff file so GitHub can display instructions for citing your work.
Choose a version: Understand common versioning approaches, including semantic versioning (v1.0.0) and calendar-based versioning (v2026.10.26).
Prepare a GitHub release: Identify a version of your project, write meaningful release notes, and prepare a release using GitHub’s interface.
Understand archival and DOIs: Explain how Zenodo can preserve a release, what a DOI identifies, and why individual versions may have different DOIs.
Make your work easier to cite: Add clear citation and version information to your README and understand how that information evolves with subsequent releases.




You’ll need:

A GitHub account and a repository you can edit. You can continue with the water-quality project from earlier Pads or use your own research repository.
A README describing your project and its contents.
A few changes already committed to your repository. These will help you think about version numbers and release notes.
No Python or command-line experience. We’ll use GitHub’s web interface for the activities.

You do not need a Zenodo account to complete the required activities. However, if you want to explore the optional publishing pathway, you’ll need a Zenodo account and permission to deposit your repository.


This Pad distinguishes between preparing a release and publishing one.
If you’re using the water-quality training project, you’ll complete the GitHub activities, including creating CITATION.cff and preparing a draft release. You’ll explore DOI creation through a simulated example rather than depositing the training repository in Zenodo.
Why? Zenodo is intended to preserve research outputs for long-term discovery and citation. Creating many permanent records of the same training exercise would add little scientific value.
If you’re working on your own research project and have the necessary permissions, you can follow the optional publishing pathway to release and archive your work.
Preparing a release does not mean your research is automatically ready to publish. Identifying missing information, unresolved scientific concerns, or permissions that need clarification is an important part of the process.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
One project, several research products
Consider our water-quality project, where we’re studying nitrate concentrations at monitoring stations.







Research product
What does it provide?




GitHub repository
The evolving project, including notebooks, documentation, history, and ongoing work.


GitHub release
An identified version of the project, linked to a Git tag, with release notes and downloadable files.


Archived version
A preserved copy of a particular version, which may be deposited in a research repository such as Zenodo and assigned a DOI.


Dataset
The underlying observations or measurements, which may have their own repository, version, and citation.


Research paper
The scientific questions, methods, results, and interpretations, with its own citation.



These products are connected, but one does not automatically replace the others.
For example, citing a paper about nitrate concentrations does not necessarily identify the exact notebook version used to produce its figures. Likewise, citing the notebook does not replace crediting the original data providers.

How do GitHub releases fit in?
A GitHub release is built around a tag, which identifies a particular point in the repository’s history.
Think of it this way:

Your main branch continues to evolve as you make changes.
A tag identifies a particular state of the files.
A GitHub release uses that tag and adds useful information, such as a version name and release notes.
A research archive such as Zenodo can preserve a version and provide a DOI for citation.

A GitHub release does not automatically create a DOI. And although GitHub provides downloadable ZIP files for releases, downloading a ZIP is not the same as depositing a version in a research archive.






TipWhen should you create a release?



That depends on what you’re developing.
For a scientific workflow, a release often accompanies a research milestone, such as a paper submission or publication. This helps preserve the exact analysis used to produce the reported results.
For research software, releases usually follow meaningful changes to the software, such as new functionality, improvements, or bug fixes. They don’t need to wait for a publication.
In both cases, the goal is to identify a version that others can reliably use. We’ll explore how to decide when a release is warranted later in this Pad.








NoteWhat about “Archive this repository” on GitHub?



GitHub also has an Archive this repository feature. It makes the repository read-only, generally indicating that development is no longer active.
This is different from preserving a particular release in Zenodo. You can continue developing your GitHub repository while archiving individual versions elsewhere.

text:
Explore your own repository
Now let’s look at the repository you’ve been working with.

Open your repository on GitHub.
Look at the files and README. What research product does the repository contain—a scientific workflow, software, documentation, or some combination?
Find Releases on the repository page (usually in the right sidebar). Open it. Do you already have any releases or tags? It’s perfectly fine if you don’t.
Return to your README. Does it tell other researchers where the input data came from? Does it reference an associated paper, if one exists?
Think about what another researcher would need to reproduce or reuse your work. Is all that information available?







TipIf you’re using the water-quality project



Your repository contains the materials from the earlier Pads, but that doesn’t mean every scientific issue has been resolved.
For example, we previously identified a problem with the order of quality-control filtering and replicate averaging. The notebook itself has not yet been corrected.
Would you want to publish a release that other researchers might treat as a validated analysis?
You don’t need to resolve this question yet. In the next part, we’ll examine what makes a repository ready for release—and what to do when it isn’t.


The key idea is that a repository represents an evolving project, while a release identifies a particular state of that project.
Neither automatically guarantees scientific quality, long-term preservation, or appropriate citation. Those require additional decisions, which we’ll explore throughout this Pad.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
What should you check?
Before releasing a research workflow or software project, consider six areas.







Area
Questions to ask




Documentation
Can someone understand what the project does, what the files contain, and where to start?


Data and provenance
Are input data identified? Can others find them and understand their sources, units, and processing?


Reproducibility
Are instructions, dependencies, and required software versions documented sufficiently for someone to use the work?


Scientific or technical correctness
Are there known errors that could affect results or users? Are important limitations documented?


Sharing permissions
Are there restricted data, credentials, third-party materials, or other constraints on what can be shared?


Authorship and responsibility
Do you know who contributed and who has authority to approve publication?



We’ll address two additional requirements later in this Pad: selecting a license and creating citation metadata. You don’t need to have those completed yet.






ImportantA known error doesn’t disappear when you make a release



Remember the water-quality project from our earlier Pads?
We identified a scientific problem: the notebook averages nitrate replicates before excluding measurements with failed quality checks. We discussed correcting the methodology, but the notebook itself has not yet been fixed.
Publishing this workflow as a validated analysis could mislead other researchers.
That doesn’t prevent us from preparing the repository for a future release. It means the correction remains an open task, and we should not publish the current notebook as a validated scientific product.
The same principle applies to software: not every open Issue prevents a release, but a bug that compromises important results or functionality may need to be resolved before publishing.

section: What should you do with your findings?
text:
What should you do with your findings?
A release-readiness review is most useful when it leads to action.
You may have identified missing instructions, data-access questions, scientific errors, or decisions that require input from other team members.
You don’t need to resolve everything during this Pad. However, important problems should be documented so they aren’t forgotten.
On GitHub:

If you found an important problem, check whether it already has an Issue.
If it does, add any useful new information or clarification. If it doesn’t, create an Issue describing the problem and what would count as resolving it.
If the problem is simply missing or inaccurate documentation that you can safely correct now, you can update the README instead.
Keep unresolved Issues open. Preparing a release is not a reason to close them.

You can paste the relevant findings from your review into an Issue, but you don’t need to create a separate Issue for every checklist item.

For the water-quality project
The unresolved QC problem should be identified as needing attention.
If you already have an Issue describing the correction, leave it open. You may want to clarify that the notebook itself still needs to be updated and that the analysis should not be represented as validated until the correction has been implemented and checked.
You can continue preparing the training repository throughout this Pad, including its citation metadata and draft release.
You will not publish the training release or mint a DOI for it.






CautionWhat if you discover information that should not have been shared?



If you discover a password, API key, restricted dataset, or other sensitive information in your repository, do not publish a release.
Deleting a file from the current repository does not necessarily remove it from Git history. Exposed credentials should be revoked or rotated, and the repository may require additional remediation.
See GitHub’s guidance on removing sensitive data before proceeding.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
Ready for the next step?
You should now have a clearer picture of what your repository contains, what still needs attention, and whether you have the information and authority needed to prepare it for sharing.
A repository doesn’t need to be perfect before you start preparing a release. But its limitations must be understood, and decisions to publish should be deliberate.
Next, we’ll examine an important distinction: just because someone can see your work doesn’t mean they have permission to reuse it. That’s where licensing comes in.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: One repository, different kinds of material
text:
One repository, different kinds of material
Research repositories often contain more than one type of material.







Material
What should you consider?




Code and notebooks
Software licenses such as MIT, BSD, Apache, or GPL may be appropriate for code you are authorized to license.


Data
Data may come with their own license, access conditions, or restrictions. Original datasets may use licenses or public-domain tools such as CC BY or CC0.


Documentation and figures
These may use licenses such as Creative Commons, or be covered by the project’s software license when appropriate.


Third-party material
You cannot simply assign a new license to material you don’t have the rights to license.



For repositories containing several kinds of material, you may need different licenses or additional notices explaining which permissions apply to which files.






ImportantLicensing and citation are not the same thing




Licensing addresses what someone is permitted to do with your work.
Citation tells someone how to credit the research product they used.

A license may include attribution requirements, but providing a citation does not automatically grant permission to reuse material. Likewise, permission to reuse something does not eliminate the need for appropriate scholarly credit.
We’ll create citation metadata in the next part.

section: Activity: Check your repository’s reuse permissions
text:
Activity: Check your repository’s reuse permissions
Return to your GitHub repository.

Step 1: Find out what is already licensed

On the Code tab, look for a file named LICENSE, LICENSE.md, or a similar name.
If one exists, open it. What does it permit, and which files does it cover?
Check your README for licensing information about code, data, documentation, or other materials.
Consider whether you have permission to distribute and license everything included in the repository.

For the water-quality project, think about the notebooks, synthetic measurements, figures, and documentation. Even when data are synthetic, you should establish who can authorize their redistribution.


Step 2: Decide what you can do
You have two possible paths.
Path A: You have permission to choose a license
If you own or have authority to license the relevant material and have already selected an appropriate license:

On GitHub, select Add file → Create new file.
Name the file LICENSE.
Select Choose a license template.
Review the available licenses and select the one you’ve decided to use.
Follow GitHub’s instructions to review and submit the license.
Commit the change, using a message such as Add project license.

If your repository includes materials covered by different licenses, clarify their scope in your README. Don’t imply that the new license covers material for which you cannot grant rights.
Return to the repository’s main page. For a recognized standard license, GitHub may display the license information in the repository’s About area.
Path B: You need more information or authorization
Perhaps your repository contains data from another institution, was developed with collaborators, or includes material whose licensing terms are unclear.
In that case, don’t choose a license just to finish the exercise.
Instead, create a GitHub Issue titled:
Confirm licensing and reuse permissions before release
In its description, identify:

Which materials need licensing clarification.
Whose permission or advice you need.
What needs to be decided before publication.

You can also add a short licensing-status statement to your README, making clear that permissions are still being reviewed.
This is a useful outcome: you’ve identified an obstacle to reuse and made it visible to the project team.






TipUsing the water-quality training repository?



You can practice examining GitHub’s license templates and record a proposed license, but only add a real license if the exercise materials give you the authority to do so.
If the permissions aren’t established, document the proposed licensing decision in a GitHub Issue rather than assigning rights you may not have.
You’ll still complete the remaining GitHub activities, including creating CITATION.cff and preparing a draft release. You won’t publish the training release or deposit it in Zenodo.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
Want to go further?
Choosing an appropriate license involves more than selecting one from a dropdown. You may need to consider license compatibility, attribution requirements, commercial reuse, derivative works, and institutional policies.
We’ll explore these decisions in a dedicated Licensing Deep End Pad.
For now, these resources can help you investigate your options:

Choose a License — an introduction to common software licenses.
Licensing a repository — GitHub Docs — guidance on how licensing works on GitHub.
Licenses for non-software material — considerations for data, documentation, and other research products.

The important outcome is that you’ve either clarified your repository’s reuse permissions or identified what still needs to be resolved.
Next, we’ll tackle the other side of sharing research: how should someone cite your work?

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
What’s in a citation file?
A CITATION.cff file can contain:







Field
Purpose




title
The name of the software, workflow, or research product


authors
The people or organizations who should receive citation credit


message
A short explanation of how you would like the work cited


repository-code
Where the source repository is located


version
The version of the research product


date-released
When that version was released


doi
A persistent identifier for the research product, if available


orcid
A persistent identifier for an individual author, if available



You don’t need every field immediately. In particular, you shouldn’t invent a release date, version, or DOI for work that hasn’t been released yet.

Who should be listed as an author?
Authorship deserves some thought.
GitHub records who contributes commits, but GitHub contributors and citation authors aren’t necessarily identical. For example, someone who helped design the scientific methodology may deserve authorship even if they never committed a file.
The author list should reflect the project’s agreed attribution practices. Author order may matter, especially in scientific research.
You can include ORCID identifiers to help distinguish researchers with similar names. These should be the actual identifiers of the authors.






TipORCID



An ORCID iD is a persistent identifier for a researcher. It helps connect publications, datasets, software, and other research contributions to the correct person, even when names change or multiple researchers have similar names.
ORCID identifiers are optional in CITATION.cff, but including them when available makes research credit more reliable.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
Activity: Create your citation file
Let’s create a citation file for your repository.

Step 1: Start with a template
If you’re using the water-quality training project, you can start with the example below. The project title and group author are illustrative; they are not claims of actual authorship.
If you’re using your own repository, replace them with the correct title and agreed authorship information.
cff-version: 1.2.0
message: "If you use this workflow, please cite it using these metadata."
title: "Water-Quality Nitrate Analysis Workflow (training example)"
authors:
  - name: "Water-Quality Training Project (example)"
repository-code: "https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY"
Replace OWNER/REPOSITORY with the information from your GitHub repository URL.
For your own research, you will usually want to list individual authors. For example, the authors section could instead look like this:
authors:
  - family-names: "FIRST_AUTHOR_FAMILY_NAME"
    given-names: "FIRST_AUTHOR_GIVEN_NAME"
  - family-names: "SECOND_AUTHOR_FAMILY_NAME"
    given-names: "SECOND_AUTHOR_GIVEN_NAME"
Replace the placeholders with the actual names, in the agreed order.
If an author has an ORCID iD, add an orcid field under their name, using the complete https://orcid.org/... URL.






NoteA few details about YAML



CITATION.cff uses YAML, a plain-text format for structured information.

Spaces and indentation matter. Use spaces, not tabs.
Each field has a name followed by a colon (:).
The - before an author marks an entry in a list.
Quotation marks help keep titles and other text containing special characters intact.

You don’t need to learn YAML in depth for this exercise. Follow the template carefully and edit the information it contains.




Step 2: Add the file to GitHub

Open your repository on GitHub and select the Code tab.
Select Add file → Create new file.
Name the file exactly CITATION.cff. It should be in the repository’s top-level directory, alongside your README.
GitHub may suggest a citation-file template. You can replace that content with the template above, adapted to your project.
Review the content, particularly the title, authors, and repository URL.
Click Commit changes… and use a message such as Add citation metadata for research workflow.
Commit the file. If you’re working on a branch, merge the change into the repository’s default branch using a pull request, as you practiced in Pad 3.

You have now added structured citation information to your research repository.


Step 3: See what GitHub does with it
Return to the repository’s main page on its default branch.
Look for Cite this repository in the right sidebar.

Select Cite this repository.
Look at the citation GitHub generates in APA format.
Examine the BibTeX citation.
Check whether the title and authors match what you intended.
If something is incorrect, edit CITATION.cff, commit the correction, and check again.







TipDon’t see “Cite this repository”?



First check that:

The filename is exactly CITATION.cff.
The file is in the repository’s root directory.
The change is present on the default branch (usually main).
The YAML structure and indentation are correct.

If GitHub still cannot interpret the file, you can use the Citation File Format initializer to construct a citation file with guided validation, or consult the CFF schema documentation.
Seeing GitHub’s citation display is a useful functional check, but it isn’t a substitute for full schema validation.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: Two different kinds of version numbers
text:
Two different kinds of version numbers
You probably noticed that our example starts with:
cff-version: 1.2.0
Does that mean your workflow is already at version 1.2.0?
No! There are two different version fields.
cff-version: 1.2.0
version: "1.0.0"

cff-version identifies the version of the Citation File Format specification. For the format used here, it remains 1.2.0 even when you update citation information.
version identifies the version of your workflow, software, or dataset. This changes when you create a new version of your research product.

You should keep the research-product version consistent with the release being described. When you create a new release, review the version, date-released, and doi fields together.
You do not need to change either version number every time you correct a typo in CITATION.cff.
For now, we haven’t added a research-product version to the training example because we haven’t created a release. We’ll revisit this in the next sections.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: What if your workflow also has a paper?
text:
What if your workflow also has a paper?
Many scientific workflows accompany a research paper, and software projects may also have a methods or software publication.
The paper and the workflow are related, but they are different research products.
For example:

The paper describes the research question, scientific results, and interpretation.
The workflow citation identifies the computational work used to generate or analyze the results.
The data citation acknowledges the measurements or other source data used in the analysis.

Depending on how someone uses the work, they may need to cite more than one of these. The paper communicates the scientific findings, while the workflow citation credits the computational methods and implementation used to produce them. Researchers should cite the workflow independently of the paper, along with the underlying datasets when appropriate.
CITATION.cff also supports a field called preferred-citation, which can instruct GitHub to recommend an associated paper instead of the repository itself.
That can be useful in some projects, but it changes what GitHub generates when someone chooses Cite this repository.
For this exercise, we’ll keep the citation focused on the workflow or software itself. Later, we’ll add clear instructions to the README explaining how to cite the repository and any associated research products.






NoteYour citation will evolve with the project



When your project receives its first versioned release, you’ll update CITATION.cff with the appropriate version and release date.
If you archive that release in Zenodo and obtain a DOI, you can update the citation information again.
Remember that GitHub displays citation information from the default branch. That information may describe the latest release, while someone reproducing an earlier study needs to cite the specific version they used.
An archived, version-specific citation helps with that distinction.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
What have you accomplished?
Your repository now tells other researchers how to give credit to the people or team responsible for the work.
You have also seen that citation metadata is separate from licensing, GitHub’s commit history, and any associated publications.
If you’re using the training repository, keep its citation clearly identified as an exercise. Do not add a fictional DOI or claim that the workflow has been scientifically validated.
Next, we’ll decide when a project deserves a new version, how to name that version, and what belongs in useful release notes.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: When should you create a release?
text:
When should you create a release?
The answer depends partly on what you’re developing.







Research workflows
Research software




Releases often accompany research milestones, such as conference presentation, paper submission or publication.
Releases often follow meaningful development milestones, such as new features, bug fixes, or important improvements.


The goal may be to preserve the exact analysis used to produce published results.
The goal may be to provide users with an identifiable, tested version of the software.


A correction that changes scientific results may warrant a new release.
An important bug fix may warrant an immediate release, even if no new features have been added.



These aren’t rigid rules. You may release a workflow before publication to support peer review, or release software alongside a paper.
The important question is whether the version represents a meaningful, identifiable state of the research product.






TipWhat about unresolved Issues?



You don’t need to close every Issue before creating a release. Some Issues represent future improvements, feature requests, or long-term research goals.
However, an unresolved issue that compromises the scientific results or essential functionality may prevent a release from being suitable for its intended purpose.
Remember our water-quality project: the notebook still averages replicates before excluding measurements with failed QC. We identified the problem, but we haven’t corrected the notebook.
That correction might eventually justify a new version. For now, we must not describe it as completed or publish the current workflow as a validated analysis.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
How do you number versions?
There isn’t one versioning system that works best for every research project. Two common approaches are semantic versioning and calendar versioning.

Semantic versioning: v1.2.3
Semantic versioning, often called SemVer, uses three numbers:


  
    1
    Major
    Breaking changes
  
  .
  
    2
    Minor
    New functionality
  
  .
  
    3
    Patch
    Compatible bug fixes
  


In software, the convention is:

Major (1 → 2): Changes that break compatibility with the previous public interface, such as removing or substantially changing an API.
Minor (2 → 3): New functionality that remains compatible with the previous interface.
Patch (3 → 4): Bug fixes that preserve compatibility.

For example, if software at v1.2.3 receives a compatible bug fix, its next version might be v1.2.4.
If a new compatible feature is introduced, it might become v1.3.0.
And if an API changes in a way that requires users to modify their existing code, it might become v2.0.0.






NoteWhat about workflows?



Workflows don’t always have a public API in the same sense as software.
You can adopt a similar numbering convention, but you should explain what major, minor, and patch changes mean for your workflow.
For example, a major change might alter the expected input structure or fundamentally change how the workflow is used.
A correction to a scientific method might appear small in the code but substantially change the results. Don’t assume that every scientific correction is automatically a minor patch.
The Semantic Versioning specification provides the formal rules for software that uses SemVer.


Version numbers beginning with 0, such as 0.1.0, are commonly used during early development. Under SemVer, 1.0.0 marks a defined public interface, not proof that the software or scientific results are error-free.
The v is a common prefix for Git tags; the three numbers are the semantic version itself.


Calendar versioning: v2026.10.26
Another approach is calendar versioning, or CalVer.
Instead of describing compatibility through version numbers, the version includes a date.
For example:
v2026.10.26



Component
Meaning




2026
Year


10
Month


26
Day



This approach can be particularly useful for scientific workflows, where releases correspond to research milestones or dated snapshots.
A workflow might have a release associated with a paper submission, followed by another release several months later incorporating additional analyses.
The date identifies when the release was made, but it doesn’t explain what changed or guarantee compatibility. That’s why release notes remain important.
Calendar versioning has several possible formats. For this Pad, we’ll use vYYYY.MM.DD. If you make multiple releases on one day, you’ll need a consistent way to keep their tags unique.
You can learn more at CalVer.org.






TipWhich should you use?



If you’re developing software with a defined API, semantic versioning often communicates compatibility more effectively.
If you’re developing a scientific workflow tied to research milestones, calendar versioning may be easier to interpret.
Neither system is mandatory. Choose a convention that makes sense for your project and use it consistently.
Don’t change an existing project’s versioning convention without a good reason.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
Activity: Investigate what’s changed
Before choosing a version, return to your GitHub repository.

Open the Code tab and look at your commit history. What changes have been made?
Review the Pull requests and Issues tabs. Which problems were actually resolved, and which remain open?
Look at the README and notebooks. What does the repository currently contain?
If the project already has releases, examine the most recent one to understand what has changed since then.

For a first release, you’re describing the initial contents and capabilities of the research product, rather than changes since a previous version.
Pay attention to the difference between work that was discussed, work that was committed, and work that was validated. They aren’t necessarily the same.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
What makes useful release notes?
Release notes tell users what they’re receiving and what they should know before using it.
For a scientific project, useful release notes often include:

Summary: What is this release intended to provide?
Contents or changes: What is included, added, corrected, or improved?
Reproducibility information: Where can someone find the data, instructions, or required dependencies?
Known limitations: What important problems or restrictions remain?

For our training project, release notes might look like this:
# Water-quality workflow — proposed v0.1.0

## Summary

Initial training version of a workflow for analyzing
nitrate concentrations at monitoring stations.

## Contents

- Nitrate analysis notebook and supporting files
- Synthetic water-quality data
- Project documentation and citation metadata

## Reproducibility

Consult the README for the repository structure,
input data information, and available instructions.

## Known limitations

The notebook has not been updated to correct the
order of quality-control filtering and replicate
averaging.

This is a training snapshot, not a validated
scientific release.
Notice that the release notes describe the existing repository. They don’t claim that the QC correction has been implemented simply because it was discussed in a pull request or Issue.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
Before you move on
You should now have:

A versioning convention appropriate for your project.
A proposed release tag that follows that convention.
Draft release notes describing what your repository currently contains and any important limitations.

You haven’t created a release yet. That’s our next step.






NoteKeep the version information consistent



When you create a release, the Git tag should identify the version you’re describing.
If your project also has a version declared in package metadata, documentation, or CITATION.cff, review those values so that users aren’t given contradictory version information.
Remember that cff-version: 1.2.0 identifies the citation-file format, not your project’s version. The research-product version field should be updated when appropriate for a new release.
We’ll revisit the release date and DOI after the release has been prepared.


Next, we’ll use GitHub’s Releases interface to turn this plan into an actual draft release—without publishing the training repository.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
From commits to a release
You’ve already learned that Git records changes through commits and that branches, such as main, allow development to continue.
A release introduces another Git concept: the tag.
A tag identifies a particular commit in your repository’s history. While main can advance as new commits are added, a version tag is intended to continue pointing to the commit selected for that version.
A GitHub release is built around that tag.







GitHub feature
What does it represent?




Commit
A recorded change or set of changes


Branch (main)
A line of development that advances as changes are added


Tag (v1.0.0)
A name identifying a specific commit


Release
A published version associated with a tag, including release notes and downloadable files


Draft release
A release being prepared but not yet published



Once a release is published, GitHub automatically offers downloadable source-code archives (ZIP and tar.gz) corresponding to its tag.






NoteA draft release isn’t a published snapshot



When you create a draft release using a new tag name, GitHub can save the draft without creating the actual Git tag until you publish.
This means the draft describes a proposed version, but the final snapshot may not yet be fixed.
If main changes before publication, the new tag could identify a different state of the project than you originally intended.
For a real publication, verify the intended commit and tag before publishing. An existing tag pointing to the reviewed commit provides a more reliable starting point.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
Activity: Prepare your first release
You’ll use the version number and release notes you prepared in Part 5.

Step 1: Check your repository
Before opening the release editor:

Open your repository on GitHub and select the Code tab.
Make sure you’re viewing the branch containing the version you want to prepare, usually main.
Confirm that the README and CITATION.cff files you prepared earlier are present.
Review the most recent commits. Are the changes you intend to include actually in this branch?
Check whether any important unresolved Issues affect how the version should be described.

If you’re preparing an actual research release, also check that its citation metadata and any project or package version information are consistent with the version you intend to tag.
You can leave date-released and doi out of CITATION.cff until you have the actual information. For the training repository, you don’t need to add a release date or DOI.






WarningRemember the water-quality QC issue



The notebook still contains the quality-control problem we identified earlier.
You can prepare a draft to practice the release process, but do not publish this workflow as a validated scientific analysis.
Your release notes should explicitly acknowledge the unresolved issue.




Step 2: Open the release editor

From your repository’s Code tab, find Releases in the right sidebar.
Click Releases.
Select Draft a new release.

You’ll see a form for selecting a tag, naming the release, and describing its contents.


Step 3: Choose a tag
Select Choose a tag.
If you already have a tag for the exact commit you intend to release, you can select it.
Otherwise:

Enter the version number you chose in Part 5, such as v0.1.0 or v2026.10.26.
Select Create new tag.
Under Target, select the branch containing the files you intend to release, usually main.

For the water-quality training project, use your proposed version number. For example:
v0.1.0
We use 0.1.0 here to communicate that the project is still under development. The version number itself does not guarantee scientific readiness.






TipTag names should be unique



Don’t reuse a tag that already identifies a different version of your project.
For published releases, tags are intended to remain stable so that users can retrieve the same version in the future.
If a previous release contains an error, the normal approach is to correct the problem and create a new version—not silently replace the old one.




Step 4: Name your release
In Release title, enter a descriptive name.
For example:
Water-quality nitrate analysis — training draft v0.1.0
For your own project, use a title that identifies the research product and version.
Remember that the tag and release title serve different purposes:

The tag is the version identifier associated with a Git commit.
The release title is a human-readable description displayed on GitHub.

They can be identical, but they don’t have to be.


Step 5: Add your release notes
In Describe this release, paste the Markdown you prepared with the release-notes builder in Part 5.
Review the text before moving on.
Does it accurately describe what is included? Does it distinguish completed changes from planned work? Are known limitations documented?
You may notice a Generate release notes button. GitHub can automatically prepare release notes based on pull requests and changes between releases.
This can be helpful, especially for software projects with many contributors. However, automatically generated notes may not explain the scientific significance of a change or the limitations of an analysis.
For this exercise, use your own release notes. You can explore the generated notes for comparison if you wish.


Step 6: Examine the other release options
You may notice several additional options.
Attach binaries
This allows you to upload additional release assets, such as compiled software or other distribution files.
You don’t need to upload the notebooks and other tracked files again. GitHub will provide source-code archives for the published release.
Set as a pre-release
A pre-release is a published release identified as not yet suitable for general use, for example an alpha or beta version of software.
A pre-release is not the same thing as a draft. It is still made available to users who have access to the repository.
For our training project, leave this option unchecked. We’re saving a draft, not publishing a pre-release.
Set as latest release
GitHub can identify which published release should be treated as the latest version. This is useful for projects with multiple releases.
You don’t need to change this setting for the training exercise.


Step 7: Save your draft
At the bottom of the release editor, you’ll find the option to Publish release or Save draft.
Select Save draft. Do not select Publish release for the water-quality training repository.
GitHub will save the release information so you can review or edit it later.
You have now prepared a real GitHub draft release!

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
Inspect your draft release
Return to Releases in your repository.
Find the draft you just created. GitHub should identify it as a draft.
Open it and check:

Is the release title correct?
Does it show the intended tag name?
Are the release notes complete and accurate?
Are the scientific limitations documented?
Is the release still marked as a Draft?

If something needs changing, use the release’s edit option to revise it.






ImportantDraft vs published release



Saving a draft does not:

Publish the research product as a release.
Guarantee that a new Git tag has already been created.
Make a published release available.
Trigger Zenodo archival or DOI creation.

Publishing a release is different.
If your public GitHub repository is already connected to Zenodo and the integration is enabled, publishing a new GitHub release will automatically trigger Zenodo to archive that version and assign it a DOI.
You don’t need to manually deposit each subsequent release. Each archived version receives its own version-specific DOI.
Before clicking Publish release, check whether your repository is connected to Zenodo. Publishing may create a permanent, publicly accessible research record, not just a GitHub release.
For the water-quality training project, stop at Save draft.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
What happens when you publish?
For your own research repository, publication may be appropriate once the release-readiness review is complete and you have the authority to share the work.
When a release is published, GitHub associates it with its tag and makes the release information available to people who can access the repository.
Users can then download the source-code archive associated with that version.
This is useful for reproducibility: rather than telling someone to download whatever happens to be on main today, you can point them to a specific released version.
Before publishing a real release, verify that:

The tag identifies the exact commit intended for publication.
The README, license information, and citation metadata are correct for that version.
The release notes accurately describe the contents and limitations.
The repository and included materials are authorized for distribution.
Any release-related automation is understood.

For this Pad, publication is optional. If you’re using the training repository, leave the release as a draft.






NoteWhat about software package registries?



Publishing a GitHub release does not automatically publish your software to a package registry such as PyPI, CRAN, or conda-forge.
A GitHub release identifies and distributes a version of the repository. A package registry provides a way to distribute and install software through its packaging ecosystem.
These processes can be connected through automation, such as GitHub Actions, but they are distinct.
We’ll explore automation in Pad 6: Automate a Task, while software packaging and distribution will be covered in the Software LilyPads.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
What have you accomplished?
You now have:

A proposed version identifier.
Release notes that describe the contents and limitations of that version.
A GitHub draft release associated with your proposed tag.
An understanding of what still needs to happen before publication.

You’ve practiced the GitHub release workflow without having to publish an unfinished research product.
Next, we’ll explore what happens after a release is published: how a research archive such as Zenodo can preserve it and assign a DOI for persistent identification and citation.
For the water-quality training project, we’ll simulate that process rather than create a permanent archive record.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: Two DOIs for one research project?
text:
Two DOIs for one research project?
When Zenodo archives the first version of a research product, it normally registers two different DOIs.
They serve different purposes.








DOI
What does it identify?
When should you use it?




Version DOI
One specific archived version, such as v1.0.0
When citing the version used for a scientific analysis or software application


Concept DOI (all versions)
The research product as a whole, across its different versions
When referring to the overall project rather than a particular release



Every subsequent archived version receives a new Version DOI, but the Concept DOI stays the same.
The Concept DOI currently directs readers to the latest archived version, while individual Version DOIs continue to identify their corresponding versions.
This distinction is crucial for reproducibility.
Imagine that your paper used version v1.0.0 of a nitrate analysis workflow. A year later, the team releases v2.0.0, which implements a different method.
Someone attempting to reproduce your published results needs the original version, not the latest one.
That’s why scientific publications should normally cite the Version DOI corresponding to the workflow or software actually used.
Read more in Zenodo’s DOI versioning documentation.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: Activity: Explore Pyleoclim releases on Zenodo
text:
Activity: Explore Pyleoclim releases on Zenodo

Notice that Zenodo provides both a description of the release and the archived files. This is a real, published research software product, not just a link to GitHub.

Step 3: See how the DOI badge differs

For example, its badge Markdown would be:
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.1205661.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1205661)
This uses the same project DOI regardless of whether you’re looking at v1.2.0, v1.3.0, or a future release.
However, if your paper used Pyleoclim v1.2.0, you should cite the DOI for that exact version:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14782981
Remember: the project-level badge helps readers discover the software, while the version-specific citation helps them reproduce the research.
Don’t copy Pyleoclim’s DOI into your own repository. When you archive your own project, use the DOIs that Zenodo assigns to it.
Notice what changes when you switch versions:

The Version DOI changes.
The Concept DOI remains identical.
Earlier versions continue to have their own persistent identifiers.

This leads to a useful convention:
Use the Version DOI for citations of a specific release, and the Concept DOI for a project-level badge in your README.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: Optional: Connect your own repository to Zenodo
text:
Optional: Connect your own repository to Zenodo
Follow these steps only if you have a real research project ready for public release.
If you’re using the water-quality training example, skip to the next section.

Step 1: Connect Zenodo to GitHub

Visit Zenodo and sign in or create an account.
Connect your GitHub account if it isn’t already connected.
Open your Zenodo profile menu and select GitHub.
Select Sync now to refresh the list of repositories.
Find the repository you want to archive.
Enable the repository using its toggle.

Zenodo should now be connected to your repository.
The repository must be public for Zenodo’s GitHub integration. If the repository belongs to a GitHub organization, the organization may need to authorize the integration.






WarningConnect before publishing



Once the integration is enabled, Zenodo automatically processes newly published GitHub releases.
Check that your repository is connected before publishing the release you want archived.
Don’t assume that enabling the integration afterward will automatically import older releases.
Also remember that publishing a release may now trigger an archival action outside GitHub.




Step 2: Publish your GitHub release
Return to the draft you prepared in Part 6.
Before publishing, verify the intended tag, files, release notes, permissions, and scientific readiness.
When everything is ready, select Publish release.
Zenodo will receive the release information and begin processing the archive.
You don’t need to manually upload the GitHub source files to Zenodo when this integration is working.


Step 3: Inspect the Zenodo record
Return to Zenodo and open the GitHub section of your account.
Find the repository and its newly processed release, then open the associated Zenodo record.
Examine:

The title and description of the research product.
The listed authors and their ORCID identifiers, when provided.
The release version and publication information.
The files that were archived.
The licensing and reuse information.
The assigned DOI identifiers.

Check that the record accurately represents the project.
Zenodo can use metadata from CITATION.cff when archiving GitHub releases. If your repository also contains .zenodo.json, Zenodo gives that file precedence, so make sure the metadata in these files isn’t contradictory.
For detailed instructions, consult Zenodo’s official GitHub integration guide.






NoteWhat exactly has Zenodo preserved?



Zenodo preserves the archived release files, not necessarily every external resource required to reproduce the work.
For example, if your notebook downloads data from a separate repository or relies on packages installed elsewhere, Zenodo doesn’t automatically preserve those resources as part of the workflow.
Your README and associated documentation should still explain how to obtain the data, configure the computational environment, and reproduce the analysis.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: Add a DOI badge to your README
text:
Add a DOI badge to your README
Once a research product has been archived, make its persistent identifier visible in GitHub.
A DOI badge is a small image that links readers to the archived record.
For a project that will have multiple releases, we recommend using the Concept DOI in the badge.
That way, you don’t need to change the project-level badge every time you publish a new version.

For a real archived project

Open the project’s record in Zenodo.
Find the DOI information and identify the Concept DOI (all versions), rather than the DOI for only the current version.
Copy the Markdown for a badge pointing to the Concept DOI. You can also adapt the example below.
Open your README on GitHub and select Edit this file (the pencil icon).
Add the badge near the top, immediately after the project title.
Commit the change.

The Markdown will look similar to this:
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.CONCEPT_ID.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.CONCEPT_ID)
Replace CONCEPT_ID with the actual numeric identifier from your project’s Concept DOI. The example above is a placeholder and won’t work until it contains a real DOI.
If Zenodo provides badge Markdown directly, check its destination before copying it. We want a badge for all versions, not only one release.






TipWhy use the Concept DOI for the badge?



Your README usually introduces the project as a whole.
A Concept DOI points readers toward the overall archived project, including its evolving set of versions.
But when you cite the exact software or workflow used in a scientific analysis, you should use the Version DOI instead.
The badge helps people discover the project; a version-specific citation helps them reproduce the research.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
Update your CITATION.cff
Remember the citation file you created in Part 4?
Now that Zenodo has archived your release, you can add its DOI and update the relevant version information.
For a real published release, your CITATION.cff might include fields like these:
cff-version: 1.2.0
message: "If you use this workflow, please cite the version used."
title: "My Research Workflow"
authors:
  - family-names: "Example"
    given-names: "Researcher"
repository-code: "https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY"
version: "1.0.0"
date-released: 2026-10-26
doi: "10.5281/zenodo.VERSION_ID"
Replace the example names, repository URL, release date, version, and DOI with your project’s actual information.
In particular:

version refers to your research product, not the CFF format.
date-released is the actual release date.
doi should contain the Version DOI for the release you’re describing.
cff-version remains 1.2.0 for the CFF specification used in this example.

If you use a tag such as v1.0.0, the CFF version can be 1.0.0. The important thing is that they unambiguously describe the same release.

Make the update on GitHub

Open CITATION.cff on your repository’s default branch.
Select Edit this file.
Add or correct the version, release date, and Version DOI.
Commit the change using a message such as Update citation metadata with Zenodo DOI.
Return to the main repository page and select Cite this repository.
Check that GitHub generates the expected citation, including the correct DOI.







NoteWhy update CITATION.cff after the release?



For the first release, the DOI generally becomes available after Zenodo processes the published GitHub release.
You can then add the DOI to CITATION.cff and the badge to your README.
These changes update the living GitHub repository. They do not retroactively change the archived files in the previous release.
That’s expected: archived versions should remain stable.
For future releases, review the version information and citation metadata before tagging, and update the DOI once Zenodo has archived the new version.
GitHub reads CITATION.cff from your default branch to display Cite this repository, so keep it aligned with the release you intend people to cite.

Consider where you would put each identifier:

The DOI identifying the overall project belongs in the README badge.

title: Release and Cite your Work
section: What happens with the next release?
text:
What happens with the next release?
Your repository will continue to evolve, and new research milestones or software improvements may justify additional releases.
When preparing a new version:

Decide what changes justify the release.
Update the research-product version and other metadata before tagging.
Create and publish a new GitHub release when the project is ready.
Let Zenodo archive the new release and assign its Version DOI.
Update CITATION.cff with the new Version DOI and release information.
Keep the same Concept DOI badge in the README.

The Concept DOI continues to identify the project across releases. Each Version DOI continues to identify its specific archived version.
This means you can develop your software or workflow over time without losing the ability to cite and reproduce earlier versions.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
What have you accomplished?
You now understand how a GitHub release can become an archived, citable research product.
You can distinguish the two kinds of Zenodo DOI and explain why they serve different purposes.
For real published research products, you also know how to connect those identifiers back to the repository using a README badge and CITATION.cff.
For the water-quality training project, you’ve practiced the workflow without creating an unnecessary permanent record.
Next, we’ll bring these ideas together and review how to maintain clear citation and release information as your research project continues to evolve.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
The next release
Remember the quality-control problem in our water-quality workflow?
We identified that the notebook averages nitrate measurements before removing observations that failed quality checks. The correction is still outstanding.
Suppose the team eventually fixes the notebook, validates the updated results, and documents the change.
That could justify a new release, especially if the correction affects the scientific conclusions.
For research software, an important bug fix or new functionality might similarly justify a release without waiting for another paper.
The process you’ve learned can be repeated whenever there’s a meaningful reason to publish a new version.

title: Release and Cite your Work
text:
What changes with each release?
Some information stays the same across versions, while other information needs to be updated.







Component
What happens with a new release?




Git tag
Create a new tag identifying the new version.


Release notes
Describe what’s new, corrected, changed, and still unresolved.


CITATION.cff
Review the authors, version, date, and version-specific DOI.


README
Update instructions, limitations, and citation information as needed.


Zenodo Version DOI
A new DOI is assigned to each newly archived version.


Zenodo Concept DOI
Stays the same across all versions. The project-level README badge can remain unchanged.


Older releases
Remain identifiable and citable. Don’t silently replace them with newer versions.




The order matters
For a repository connected to Zenodo, the typical sequence is:

Before the release: Complete and validate the changes. Update the project version and citation metadata. Make sure the new release’s metadata does not incorrectly point to the previous version’s DOI.
Publish the release: Create the new tag and GitHub release once the project is ready. If Zenodo integration is enabled, it can automatically archive the release.
After archival: Obtain the new Version DOI from Zenodo and update CITATION.cff and the README’s citation instructions.
Check the result: Confirm that GitHub’s Cite this repository displays the intended citation and that the README links are correct.

Remember that CITATION.cff on the default branch normally describes the version you currently recommend citing. Earlier publications should continue citing the specific versions they used.






NoteDon’t confuse a new commit with a new release



You don’t need to change the research-product version in CITATION.cff after every commit.
During development, you may make dozens of commits before creating another release.
When preparing a new version, however, check that the version metadata matches the research product being released.
And remember: cff-version: 1.2.0 describes the citation-file format. It isn’t your software or workflow version.

text:

Return to your GitHub repository one last time.

Step 1: Review what you’ve prepared

My README explains what the project contains and how to get started.
I’ve reviewed the project’s reuse permissions and added a license where appropriate, or documented what still needs approval.
My CITATION.cff identifies the research product and its agreed authors.
I can find Cite this repository on GitHub and check the generated citation.

I’ve prepared release notes describing the actual contents and known limitations.
I’ve saved a GitHub draft release, without publishing anything that isn’t ready.
I understand the distinction between a Version DOI and a Concept DOI.

If you’ve published and archived your own research product, also verify that your DOI badge, citation metadata, and Zenodo record point to the intended research product and versions.
You don’t need a real DOI to complete this checklist.


Step 2: Identify what would justify the next release
Open your repository’s Issues tab.
Find an unresolved scientific or technical Issue and consider:

Would resolving this Issue warrant a new release, or could it wait for a larger research milestone?
What would need to be tested or validated before that release?
Would the change affect existing users or previously published scientific results?

For the water-quality example, revisit the outstanding QC correction.
Once that correction has actually been implemented and validated, a new version could document the methodological change and any impact on the results.
You can record release-related tasks in the existing Issue if useful. Don’t close the Issue until the underlying work is genuinely resolved.
This connects the planning practices from Pad 4 with the release process you’ve learned here.

text: This is the full version of the Correlations scenario from the LilyPad Are Methods Actionable?. The LilyPad version focuses on what the paper’s description leaves ambiguous; here you make all the choices that go into the analysis, including whether the correlation is statistically significant, something the original paper never tested.

title: Correlations: The Deep End
text:
Reproducible, robust, replicable
These words are used in different, sometimes opposite, ways across fields. A helpful way to keep them apart, following The Turing Way Community (2022), is to ask whether the data and the analysis are the same as in the original study or different:




Same data
Different data




Same analysis
Reproducible
Replicable


Different analysis
Robust
Generalisable



The LilyPad version asks whether the result is reproducible: can you get it from the paper’s description alone? This version goes further. Changing the smoothing, detrending, correlation measure or significance test asks whether the result is robust to other reasonable analysis choices. Extending the record to the present asks whether it is replicable with data the authors didn’t have. (Strictly speaking, all versions use today’s datasets rather than the ones available in 1991, which have since been revised.)






NoteInstructions



The goal of the exercise is to determine whether the methods described below are sufficient to reproduce the results shown in Figure 1, and how strongly the conclusions depend on choices the paper leaves open. As you work, take careful notes about what information is missing from the methods section that would help you reproduce the results.


A famous example of how scientifically impactful the details of a workflow can be is the study of Friis-Christensen & Lassen (1991), who reported a striking match between the length of the solar cycle and Northern Hemisphere land temperature. Later, Laut (2003) showed that the result hinged entirely on how the data were processed. In this example, you will tinker with parts of that workflow to understand just how brittle the results are when the workflow is ambiguous.
Here is everything the paper says about how the two series were prepared:

“[W]e have used the land air temperature for the Northern Hemisphere, expressed as anomalies relative to the interval 1951 to 1980, smoothed by Jones [see (10)].”


“We determined the length of the sunspot cycle using epochs of maxima and minima found by the secular smoothing procedure introduced by Gleissberg (12) (Fig. 2). This procedure corresponds to the application of a low-pass filter with coefficients 1, 2, 2, 2, 1 to the series of individual sunspot maximum and minimum epochs. This particular filter was selected because it has been generally used in the determination of long-term trends in solar activity, but the use of a different filter would not change the results significantly, as long as the short-term variations related to the 11-year cycle and shorter periods are removed. For the last two extrema, the available data do not allow full smoothing. Therefore, we filtered the second to last extrema by estimating the next extremum (because this is included in the filtering with a weight of one-eighth only); the last extrema express the unfiltered epochs.”


Figure captions: “The symbols (*) represent average values of the temperature record corresponding to individual solar cycles from solar maximum to solar minimum and from solar minimum to solar maximum, respectively.” “Variation of the sunspot cycle length (left-hand scale) determined as the difference between the actual smoothed sunspot extremum and the previous one. The cycle length is plotted at the central time of the actual cycle (+). The unsmoothed last values of the time series have been indicated with a different symbol (*) which represents, as in Fig. 1, the Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies.”

And here is how the result is reported:

“Furthermore, a strikingly good agreement between these two curves is revealed. There is a close association between the two curves in the up-going trends from 1900 to 1940 and since 1970, as well as in the important decrease from 1945 to 1970.”

The paper gives no quantitative measure of association (e.g. a correlation coefficient) and no test of statistical significance. Figure 1 below re-creates its central figure with today’s versions of the data.



Figure 1. Solar cycle length (blue, inverted axis: shorter cycles plotted upward) and Northern Hemisphere land temperature (red), 1850–1990, re-created after Fig. 2 of Friis-Christensen & Lassen (1991).

Collaborate on GitHub
text:
Research is rarely a solitary activity. A colleague may notice that a dataset needs better documentation, question an analysis decision, or suggest a clearer way to present results. But how do we make these improvements without disrupting someone else’s work? And how do we preserve the discussions and decisions that led to a change?
GitHub provides a way to propose, discuss, and review changes before incorporating them into a shared project. In this LilyPad, you’ll use branches and pull requests to improve your own repository while participating in a simulated collaboration on a scientific research project. You’ll discover that contributing to research involves more than writing code: reviewing documentation, questioning scientific assumptions, and providing constructive feedback are equally valuable.


By the end of this LilyPad, you will be able to:

Work on a branch: Create and manage a branch in GitHub Desktop to propose changes without directly modifying main.
Propose an improvement: Make a focused change, commit and publish it, and open a pull request on GitHub.
Review scientific changes: Examine changes to documentation and Jupyter notebooks, recognizing which changes may affect scientific interpretation or reproducibility.
Participate in a review: Use comments, approvals, and requests for changes to provide constructive feedback.
Respond to feedback: Revise your work and update an existing pull request.
Merge and synchronize: Incorporate an accepted change into main and update your local repository.




For this LilyPad, you’ll need:

A GitHub account and GitHub Desktop installed on your computer.
The research repository you created in Starting a Research Repository on GitHub and cloned to your computer in Save and Share Changes on GitHub.
A small improvement you could make to your project, such as clarifying documentation, adding information about your data, or correcting an explanation.

You don’t need to know Python or find a collaborator to complete this LilyPad.
You’ll work in two environments:

Your own repository on GitHub: You’ll create a branch, make a change, open a pull request, and eventually merge it.
An interactive research scenario in The Pond: You’ll take part in a fictional collaboration, reviewing proposed changes and responding to scientific questions through activities that simulate GitHub’s interface.

text:
Keeping shared work stable
When you create a GitHub repository, it typically starts with a branch named main. Think of this as the primary version of your research project.
A branch allows you to work on a proposed change without immediately incorporating it into main. You can experiment, revise your work, and ask others to review it before deciding whether the change should become part of the shared project.
For example, your team might have:

main — the primary version of the study.
improve-data-documentation — a branch for clarifying the data descriptions.
update-analysis-methods — another branch for improving the analysis notebook.

All three branches belong to the same repository. Changes made and committed to one branch don’t automatically become part of the others.
Branches make it easier to work on different improvements independently. Later, a pull request will allow you to propose incorporating your branch’s changes into main.
